transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. What brings you in to see me?

Well... I guess I'm here because I keep forgetting things. Important things. Like my heart follow-up appointments, or... returning calls to the clinic. Sometimes I'll even try to do a repair job around the house and realize I didn't bring the right tools. Just... stuff like that.
Over the past few months, have you also been feeling unusually sad, down, or lacking interest and energy in things you normally enjoy?
No... I wouldn't say that. I'm not sad or anything. Energy is fine, mostly. Just... what I mentioned before.
When did you first start noticing these memory issues, and have they been getting gradually worse over time, or have they stayed pretty much the same?

It's been... I guess about a year and two months. That's when it started causing real trouble, anyway. I had a... a cardiac scare back then. They made me cut back on my walking, and all the projects I used to do. Those things used to keep me settled, I suppose. So... yeah. Since then.
Have your family or friends noticed you forgetting conversations, repeating questions, or having other memory lapses that you yourself didn't notice?
No... I don't think so. Nobody has mentioned anything like that to me. I don't repeat questions or... whatever. It's just the things I already told you about.
Have these memory issues caused you any real problems handling day-to-day tasks, like managing your medications, paying bills, or finishing projects you start?

Well... I suppose it's caused some issues. The repair group at the senior center... they can't really count on me like they used to. I just don't finish things. And... the doctor's office called a few times. I guess I missed some follow-ups for my heart. So... yeah, it's been a problem.
Besides forgetting things, have you noticed any trouble concentrating, staying focused on tasks, or thinking through problems clearly?

Well... I suppose a little. Sometimes if I'm at the bridge table, or... at a planning meeting for the Fix-It Friends. I sit down meaning to pay close attention, but... after a little while, my mind just sort of slides off. Then I realize I missed half of what was said. So... yes. That happens.

Since your cardiac scare, have you noticed any episodes of dizziness, lightheadedness, or feeling like you weren't getting enough blood flow to your head—especially around the time your memory or focus issues started?
No... I don't think so. I haven't had any dizziness or... lightheadedness. Nothing like that.
Can you tell me more about that cardiac scare—did you lose consciousness, or did the doctors mention your heart stopping or your oxygen levels dropping at any point?
No... I didn't pass out. And they never said anything about my heart stopping, or... oxygen dropping. Nothing like that. I was awake.
Have you noticed any other changes, like trouble finding the right words when speaking, getting confused about directions or familiar places, or feeling disoriented about the day or time?
No... I haven't noticed anything like that. I know what day it is, and... I don't get lost or anything. My words are fine. So, no. Just what I mentioned before.
Since your cardiac scare, have you found yourself frequently worrying or preoccupied about your heart health, even during activities like the repair group or bridge games?
No... not really. I don't sit around thinking about it. When I'm at the group or playing cards, I'm just... doing that. So, no.
Did your doctors do any brain imaging or tests around the time of your cardiac scare, and if so, did they find any abnormalities—like a small stroke or reduced blood flow to your brain?
No... they didn't do any of that. They were just focused on the heart. Nobody said anything to me about my brain, or... a stroke. So, no.
Since your cardiac scare, did your doctors start you on any new medications or change the doses of medications you were already taking?
No... I don't think so. They just... kept everything the same. I'm not taking anything new.
Since your cardiac scare, have you noticed any changes in your sleep—like snoring loudly, gasping for breath, or feeling unusually tired during the day even after a full night's sleep?
No... I sleep about the same as always. I haven't noticed any gasping or... anything like that. Just regular sleep, I guess.
What exactly did the doctors tell you was wrong with your heart during that scare—was it a heart attack, an arrhythmia, heart failure, or something else?
I'm not really sure... they just said it was a scare. They didn't use any of those words, or if they did, I don't remember. Just... a scare.
Has anyone ever given you a formal memory or cognitive test—like asking you to remember a list of words, draw a clock, or count backward—and if so, do you know how you did?
No... I don't think so. Nobody's ever asked me to draw a clock or... do any of that stuff. Just regular checkups.
Would you be willing to do a quick memory test with me right now—like repeating a short list of words and recalling them a few minutes later—so I can see how your memory performs directly?
I suppose so... if it's quick. I don't really see why, but... yeah, that's fine.
Okay, let's do that now: I'm going to say three words—apple, table, and coin—please repeat them back to me, and I'll ask you to recall them again in a few minutes.
Apple... table... coin. Okay.
It's been a few minutes now—can you tell me the three words I asked you to remember earlier?
Apple... and... no. I don't know. They're gone.
Let me give you a hint: one of the words was a type of fruit. Does that help you remember what it was?
Yeah... apple. I just said that one. Doesn't help with the rest of them.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I would be willing to participate in a quick memory test right now. There is no specific symptom profile item for agreeing to or taking a memory test.

patient.answer: I suppose so... if it's quick. I don't really see why, but... yeah, that's fine.

inference.note: No new ruling-out information; awaiting objective memory test results before narrowing further.

doctor.intent: Directly assess objective memory performance to determine if there is a true amnestic deficit versus isolated attention/executive complaints, which helps distinguish mild neurocognitive impairment from other cognitive symptom categories
doctor.question: Okay, let's do that now: I'm going to say three words—apple, table, and coin—please repeat them back to me, and I'll ask you to recall them again in a few minutes.

target_item.reason: The doctor is conducting a memory test (asking the patient to repeat words), which is a clinical assessment task and does not correspond to a specific ADHD symptom profile item.

inference.note: No new information ruling out or confirming candidates; awaiting delayed recall results from memory test to assess for objective cognitive impairment before narrowing further.

doctor.intent: Assess delayed recall to determine if there's a true memory encoding/retrieval deficit versus an attention/concentration issue
doctor.question: It's been a few minutes now—can you tell me the three words I asked you to remember earlier?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking me to recall the three words from the memory test (apple, table, coin). This is an in-session cognitive task, which is not covered by any specific symptom profile item.

patient.answer: Apple... and... no. I don't know. They're gone.

inference.note: Objective memory testing now shows clear recall failure (only partial word recall), supporting genuine cognitive impairment rather than isolated amnesia. This strengthens F06.7 (mild neurocognitive disorder due to medical condition, temporally linked to cardiac event and reduced activity) and R41.8 (unspecified cognitive symptoms) while ruling out R41.3, since the pattern involves attention/executive dysfunction and functional decline rather than isolated amnesia.

doctor.intent: Determine if memory failure is due to true encoding/storage deficit (organic amnestic process) vs. retrieval/attention problem, by testing whether cueing improves recall
doctor.question: Let me give you a hint: one of the words was a type of fruit. Does that help you remember what it was?

target_item.reason: The doctor is administering a cognitive test (memory recall with a semantic cue) and asking if the hint helps the patient remember the word. This specific cognitive testing procedure is not covered by any of the ADHD symptom profile items.

patient.answer: Yeah... apple. I just said that one. Doesn't help with the rest of them.

inference.note: Objective memory testing now confirms genuine impairment (failed free recall and cued recall of 2/3 words), consistent with an objectively demonstrable cognitive deficit rather than a vague subjective complaint. Combined with functional decline (missed appointments, unfinished projects) but intact orientation, language, and instrumental functioning otherwise, this fits Mild Cognitive Disorder due to a medical condition (F06.7), likely related to the cardiac event (possible hypoperfusion/vascular contribution). R41.8 is ruled out since the cognitive symptoms are no longer just subjective but objectively confirmed on testing.

opening_question.intent: Identify the primary reason for the visit today
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. What brings you in to see me?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient shows objectively verified memory and attention deficits (poor delayed recall on 3-word test, forgetfulness, distractibility, difficulty completing tasks) emerging in temporal relation to a defined general medical event (a 'cardiac scare' about 14 months ago). There is functional impairment (missed medical follow-ups, inability to complete repair projects, unreliability in group activities), but no evidence of aphasia, disorientation, apraxia, or agnosia, and no collateral reports of memory lapses noticed by others, arguing against a major neurocognitive disorder (dementia). No hypoxic/ischemic brain injury, stroke, or loss of consciousness was confirmed, and no anxiety, depressive, or mood symptoms are present, arguing against generalized anxiety or depressive disorder. The clinical picture—mild, objectively demonstrable cognitive impairment secondary to a medical condition without meeting full dementia criteria—best fits Mild Cognitive Disorder due to a known physiological condition (F06.7).
